summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia is among the most developed in Latin America. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

Formal protections extend to partnership and family life. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in March 2016, after which the National Registry issued a memorandum ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country; couples presenting a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses. A visitor travelling with a same-sex spouse therefore has an established route to spousal recognition, including at the visa stage.

Violence against trans people remains the sharpest gap between law and experience. More than 40 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and 13 trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025 alone. In April 2025 the killing of Sara Millerey, 32, in Bello near Medellín drew national attention: a 28-second video circulating since 5 April shows her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim, before drowning. Her mother Sandra Borja said "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities.

The pattern is not confined to individual attacks. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers since March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals, stating that all listed will be military targets and naming homosexuals, lesbians, rapists and trans people. In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announced a "social cleansing" of drug addicts, prostitutes and gay men; a trans salon owner, Tatiana Cespedes, was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few economic options beyond sex work. Reporting in July 2024 and August 2025 describes these killings as calculated rather than incidental, persisting through the country's long armed conflict.

International and domestic oversight bodies have recorded the same divergence. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with killings rising. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee has also noted concern.

Access to public and commercial premises is protected by court order. Judgment T-314 of 2011 held a hotel's refusal of access to homosexuals at two events discriminatory, judgment T-909 of 2011 ordered mall guards in Cali to take a course so as not to repress people expressing affection in public, and judgment T-301 of 2004 ordered Santa Marta police to stop harassing homosexuals at the city boardwalk. Detention is addressed by specific rulings: a 2011 Constitutional Court decision allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a further court ruling protected the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty in its treatment of trans detainees.
tangentialFactors:
Colombian society remains generally conservative despite supportive media coverage, including gay characters in prime-time programming. A bloc of conservative senators defeated a civil union bill in Congress on 19 June 2007, and the country's Inspector General asked the Constitutional Court in 2015 to invalidate all same-sex marriages approved in Colombia. By 31 March 2016 a campaign to force a referendum repealing the November 2015 same-sex adoption ruling had gathered 1.8 million signatures including 45 members of Congress; a congressional committee shelved it 20 to 12 in May 2017. An Invamer poll of October 2019 put same-sex marriage support at 50% against 47% opposed and adoption at 36% in favour against 62% opposed, while 2016 polls showed 37% to 40% support for marriage and only 22% for adoption.

Legislative protection is uneven in areas that affect trans people directly. A 2011 law penalises discrimination based on sexual orientation with one to three years' imprisonment plus fines. Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed: the Inconvertibles bill of Congressperson Mauricio Toro, introduced 10 May 2022, had failed by 2024, and Congressperson Carolina Giraldo proposed the similar bill Quiérele siempre in 2025. Consensual same-sex sexual activity was decriminalised in 1981, and Judgment C-507 of 1999 declared unconstitutional the military prohibition on homosexual acts, but as of 2020 military culture still discouraged discussion of same-sex attraction under a "se puede ser, pero no demostrar" norm.

Comparison with the wider region is favourable on paper: marriage since 2016, adoption since 2015, and identification change without medical examinations place Colombia ahead of most Latin American jurisdictions in formal terms. The UN Independent Expert's May 2025 mission explicitly framed the country as a regional leader in legislation while documenting that the legislative lead has not carried into protection from lethal violence. Bogotá and Medellín have established gay neighbourhoods, bars, and counselling and legal advice centres, which contrasts with the situation in Caquetá and Guajira where armed groups operate openly against named individuals.
localsOnly:
For Colombian residents, the sex marker on government-issued identification is changed by signing a document before a notary, a route available since the June 2015 rule change and not requiring judicial authorisation, bodily inspection or psychiatric assessment. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 grounds recognition in self-identification without a surgical requirement, and the 2016 report Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS at Universidad de los Andes, recommended ending psychiatric pathologization of transgender identity and abandoning sterilisation as a prerequisite for other physical changes.

Residents benefit from a dense layer of institutional obligations. The 2016 Ministry of Interior presidential decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture. The Constitutional Court extended social security health insurance benefits to same-sex couples on 5 October 2007 and pension rights on 17 April 2008. Since 2014 LGBTQ individuals can adopt their partner's biological child, the 4 November 2015 ruling granted full same-sex adoption rights barring agency discrimination, and a 12 November 2015 ruling required birth registration listing two mothers or two fathers.

Education and anti-discrimination machinery is resident-facing. In 1998 the Constitutional Court ruled that public school teachers cannot be fired for revealing their sexual orientation and that private religious schools cannot ban gay students from enrolling. After student Sergio Urrego committed suicide in August 2014 following discrimination by his teachers, the Constitutional Court ruled for his family and ordered the Ministry of Education to review, within a year, the coexistence manuals of all schools nationwide so that no article discriminates against children by sexual orientation or gender identity. In 2012 the Court found that sexual orientation cannot be a criterion for preventing blood donation and ordered the Ministry of Health and Social Protection to rewrite donation regulations so that they assess risk by sexual behaviour rather than orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
A comprehensive trans law was still under consideration at the time of the most recent source material, and its status, scope and any enacted provisions are unresolved in this inventory. Whether the trans and non-binary markers introduced on national identification documents in November 2025 are implemented uniformly across all issuing offices, and whether any downstream agency applies them consistently, is not sourced here.

Conversion therapy bans remain unpassed as of 2025, with two bills before Congress and no enacted prohibition; the current legal position on the practice is therefore unresolved beyond the absence of a statute. The killing figures in this record come from different bodies covering different periods and definitions, 40-plus transgender women in 2023, 13 trans people in the first quarter of 2025, and 35 LGBTI murders from January to May 2025 recorded by the Attorney General's Office, and they are not reconciled into a single series.

Risk varies sharply by department and is not systematically mapped in these sources: Caquetá and Guajira show organised armed-group campaigns against named individuals, while Bogotá and Medellín have established community infrastructure. Whether court orders on access to public and commercial premises, and the rulings on treatment of trans detainees, are enforced consistently outside major cities is not sourced. The outcome of the Millerey investigation ordered by President Petro in April 2025, and the disposition of the 15 former rebels indicted by the Special Jurisdiction for Peace in July 2023, are unresolved in this inventory.
